CALCULUS

MADE CLEAR

The Easiest, Fastest Step-by-Step Path
from “I Don’t Get It” to “Now I See It”

ONE PROMISE You will learn what calculus means, why its rules work, and how to solve problems—one small idea at a time.

A beginner-first learning guide prepared for Sunday Pastores

sections.title: How to Use This Book
sections.html:
How to Use This Book

Calculus becomes difficult when symbols arrive before meaning. This book reverses that order: picture first, plain language second, symbols third, practice fourth. Read with pencil and paper. Pause before each answer. If a step feels mysterious, return to the sentence immediately before it—the missing idea is usually there.

Read one chapter at a time. Speed comes from clarity, not rushing.

Copy every worked example by hand. Your brain notices structure while your hand writes.

Say the meaning aloud: derivative means instant rate; integral means accumulated total.

Attempt every practice problem before checking the answer key.

Use the 20-minute plan: 12 minutes reading, 6 minutes solving, 2 minutes explaining the idea in your own words.

PERMISSION You do not need to be a “math person.” You need only to understand the next step.

sections.title: CHAPTER 1
sections.html:
CHAPTER 1

The Tiny Algebra Toolkit

YOUR GOAL Refresh only the algebra calculus uses.

The Big Idea

Calculus is not “advanced arithmetic.” It is a way to describe change and accumulation. But algebra is its grammar. You need a small, dependable toolkit—not every technique you ever saw in school.

Variables, powers, and order

A variable is a placeholder for a number. In x², the 2 says multiply x by itself. Negative exponents mean reciprocals: x⁻² = 1/x². Fractional exponents mean roots: x¹ᐟ² = √x.

Follow parentheses, exponents, multiplication/division, then addition/subtraction. The expression 3(x+2)² means: add first, square second, multiply by 3 last.

The three moves you will use constantly

Simplify: combine like terms, such as 3x+2x=5x. Factor: reverse multiplication, such as x²−9=(x−3)(x+3). Solve: perform the same legal operation on both sides until the variable stands alone.

Fractions obey one key idea: you may cancel factors, not terms. In x(x+2)/x, cancel x to get x+2 when x≠0. In (x+2)/x, you cannot cancel the x inside the sum.

Slope before calculus

Between two points, slope = rise/run = change in y divided by change in x. Using points (2,5) and (6,13), slope=(13−5)/(6−2)=8/4=2. This average rate is the doorway to derivatives.

Worked Example

Problem: Simplify (x²−9)/(x−3), assuming x≠3.

1 Factor the numerator: x²−9=(x−3)(x+3).

2 Rewrite the fraction as (x−3)(x+3)/(x−3).

3 Cancel the common factor x−3.

Answer: x+3. The original expression is still undefined at x=3, even though the simplified expression has a value there.

Common Mistakes

Cancelling terms across addition. Factor first.

Forgetting that x⁰=1 (for x≠0).

Changing only one side of an equation.

Practice: Do It Yourself

1. Simplify 4x+7−2x+3.

2. Factor x²−16.

3. Solve 3x+5=20.

4. Find the slope through (1,4) and (5,12).

5. Rewrite x⁻³ without a negative exponent.

CHAPTER IN ONE BREATH Calculus needs a compact algebra toolkit: simplify, factor, solve, work with powers, and compute slope.

sections.title: CHAPTER 2
sections.html:
CHAPTER 2

Functions: Machines with Inputs and Outputs

YOUR GOAL Read, evaluate, and interpret function notation.

The Big Idea

A function is a reliable machine: each allowed input produces exactly one output. The notation f(x) does not mean f times x. It means “the output of function f when the input is x.”

Evaluating a function

If f(x)=x²+3x, then f(2)=2²+3(2)=4+6=10. Replace every x with the chosen input, using parentheses.

The difference f(b)−f(a) measures how much the output changes while the input moves from a to b. Dividing by b−a gives average rate of change.

Domain and range

The domain is the set of allowed inputs. Avoid division by zero and square roots of negative numbers when working with real numbers. The range is the set of outputs the function can actually produce.

Four useful families

Linear functions have constant slope. Quadratics bend like U-shapes. Exponentials change by a constant percentage. Trigonometric functions repeat in cycles. Calculus gives a common language for all of them.

Worked Example

Problem: For f(x)=x²−1, find the average rate of change from x=2 to x=5.

1 Compute f(2)=4−1=3.

2 Compute f(5)=25−1=24.

3 Divide output change by input change: (24−3)/(5−2)=21/3.

Answer: 7 units of output per unit of input.

Common Mistakes

Reading f(3) as multiplication.

Replacing only some occurrences of x.

Ignoring units: a rate should usually have “per” in its units.

Practice: Do It Yourself

1. If f(x)=2x²+1, find f(3).

2. For g(x)=1/(x−4), which input is forbidden?

3. Find the average rate of f(x)=3x+2 from x=1 to x=6.

4. If C(t) is cost after t months, explain C(12)−C(5).

CHAPTER IN ONE BREATH A function connects an input to one output; calculus studies how that output changes and accumulates.

sections.title: CHAPTER 3
sections.html:
CHAPTER 3

Graphs: Seeing a Function

YOUR GOAL Translate among a story, a formula, a table, and a graph.

The Big Idea

A graph is a movie of a function compressed into one picture. Moving left to right means the input increases. Height shows output. Steepness shows how fast output is changing.

Reading shape

A graph is increasing where it rises as x moves right and decreasing where it falls. A peak is a local maximum; a valley is a local minimum. A straight segment has constant slope; a curve has changing slope.

Secant versus tangent

A secant line crosses a curve at two points and shows average change. A tangent line touches the curve locally and shows instant change. Calculus turns secants into tangents by moving the two points infinitely close.

Units tell the story

If vertical position is miles and horizontal time is hours, slope is miles per hour. If vertical cost is dollars and horizontal quantity is items, slope is dollars per item. Always attach meaning to slope.

Worked Example

Problem: A tank rises from 20 gallons at minute 2 to 44 gallons at minute 8. Find and interpret the secant slope.

1 Find the vertical change: 44−20=24 gallons.

2 Find the horizontal change: 8−2=6 minutes.

3 Divide: 24/6=4.

Answer: The tank gained an average of 4 gallons per minute.

Common Mistakes

Confusing height with slope. A high graph can be falling.

Assuming a curve has one slope everywhere.

Leaving the final rate without units.

Practice: Do It Yourself

1. A car goes from 30 miles to 90 miles between hour 1 and hour 3. Find average velocity.

2. If a graph rises but becomes flatter, is its slope positive or negative? Is slope increasing or decreasing?

3. What does a horizontal tangent suggest about instantaneous change?

CHAPTER IN ONE BREATH Height tells how much; slope tells how fast; curvature tells how the rate itself is changing.

sections.title: CHAPTER 4
sections.html:
CHAPTER 4

Limits: Getting as Close as We Want

YOUR GOAL Understand a limit as a nearby trend, not blind substitution.

The Big Idea

A limit asks: “What value does the output approach as the input approaches a target?” It cares about nearby behavior. The function may have a hole, a jump, or no defined value at the target.

The approach idea

lim x→a f(x)=L means we can make f(x) as close to L as we want by taking x sufficiently close to a (without requiring x=a). Check from both left and right. The two-sided limit exists only when both sides approach the same value.

Three practical methods

First try direct substitution. If it gives an ordinary number, you are usually done. If it gives 0/0, simplify by factoring or rationalizing. If left and right disagree, the two-sided limit does not exist.

Why limits matter

Instantaneous speed seems impossible because speed uses a time interval. Limits solve this: calculate average speed over smaller and smaller intervals and identify the number approached. That limiting number is instantaneous speed.

Worked Example

Problem: Evaluate lim x→3 (x²−9)/(x−3).

1 Direct substitution gives 0/0. This is a signal to simplify, not an answer.

2 Factor x²−9=(x−3)(x+3).

3 For x≠3, cancel x−3, leaving x+3.

4 Now let x approach 3: x+3 approaches 6.

Answer: 6. The original function may have a hole at x=3, but its nearby values approach 6.

Common Mistakes

Calling 0/0 the answer. It means “do more work.”

Checking only one side of a jump.

Thinking a function must be defined at a for its limit at a to exist.

Practice: Do It Yourself

1. Evaluate lim x→2 (x²−4)/(x−2).

2. Evaluate lim x→5 (2x+1).

3. If the left-hand limit is 3 and the right-hand limit is 7, does the two-sided limit exist?

4. Explain in words why a hole does not automatically destroy a limit.

CHAPTER IN ONE BREATH A limit describes the destination of nearby values; it is the precision tool that makes instantaneous change possible.

sections.title: CHAPTER 5
sections.html:
CHAPTER 5

The Derivative: Speed at One Instant

YOUR GOAL Build the derivative from average rate of change.

The Big Idea

The derivative is the answer to one question: “How fast is the output changing right now?” Geometrically, it is tangent slope. In motion, it is instantaneous velocity. Economically, it is marginal change.

From average to instant

For f(x), average rate from x to x+h is [f(x+h)−f(x)]/h. As h approaches 0, the second point approaches the first. The limit is f′(x), the derivative.

Notation that says the same thing

f′(x), y′, and dy/dx all name a derivative. The notation dy/dx reminds us that it measures tiny output change per tiny input change.

Meaning of the sign

If f′(x)>0, f is locally increasing. If f′(x)<0, it is locally decreasing. If f′(x)=0, the graph has a horizontal tangent—but it might be a peak, valley, or flat crossing.

Worked Example

Problem: Use the definition to find the derivative of f(x)=x².

1 Write [f(x+h)−f(x)]/h = [(x+h)²−x²]/h.

2 Expand: (x+h)²=x²+2xh+h².

3 Subtract x²: [2xh+h²]/h.

4 Factor and cancel h: h(2x+h)/h=2x+h.

5 Let h approach 0.

Answer: f′(x)=2x. At x=3, the tangent slope is 6.

Common Mistakes

Setting h=0 before cancelling; that creates division by zero.

Confusing f′(x) with f(x). One is slope; the other is height.

Assuming derivative zero always means a maximum.

Practice: Do It Yourself

1. Using f′(x)=2x, find the slope of y=x² at x=5.

2. Use the definition to differentiate f(x)=3x+2.

3. If position s(t)=t² meters, find velocity at t=4.

4. What does f′(7)=−3 mean in plain language?

CHAPTER IN ONE BREATH The derivative is the limit of average rates over shrinking intervals: tangent slope and instantaneous rate are the same idea.

sections.title: CHAPTER 6
sections.html:
CHAPTER 6

Derivative Rules Without the Mystery

YOUR GOAL Differentiate common functions quickly and accurately.

The Big Idea

The definition explains the derivative; rules make it fast. Each rule is a compressed result proven from limits. Learn the pattern, then attach meaning.

Power, constant, and sum rules

Power rule: d/dx(xⁿ)=n·xⁿ⁻¹. Bring the exponent down and reduce it by one. Constants differentiate to 0 because they do not change. Differentiate sums term by term.

Thus d/dx(4x³−2x+7)=12x²−2.

Product and quotient rules

Product: (uv)′=u′v+uv′. Both factors get a turn changing. Quotient: (u/v)′=(u′v−uv′)/v². Keep the subtraction order.

Exponential and trig essentials

d/dx(eˣ)=eˣ. d/dx(sin x)=cos x. d/dx(cos x)=−sin x. These trig rules assume x is measured in radians.

Worked Example

Problem: Differentiate y=(x²+1)(3x−4).

1 Let u=x²+1 and v=3x−4.

2 Compute u′=2x and v′=3.

3 Use u′v+uv′: 2x(3x−4)+(x²+1)3.

4 Expand: 6x²−8x+3x²+3.

Answer: y′=9x²−8x+3.

Common Mistakes

Using (uv)′=u′v′. That is not the product rule.

Forgetting that the derivative of a constant is zero.

Reducing the exponent but forgetting to multiply by the old exponent.

Practice: Do It Yourself

1. Differentiate 5x⁴−3x²+8.

2. Differentiate (x+1)(x²−2).

3. Differentiate (x²+1)/x.

4. Differentiate sin x+eˣ.

CHAPTER IN ONE BREATH Derivative rules are reliable shortcuts: power for powers, sum term by term, and special rules for products, quotients, exponentials, and trig functions.

sections.title: CHAPTER 7
sections.html:
CHAPTER 7

The Chain Rule: Changes Inside Changes

YOUR GOAL Differentiate a function nested inside another function.

The Big Idea

Many formulas are machines inside machines. If distance depends on radius and radius depends on time, distance changes because radius changes. The chain rule multiplies those rates.

Outside then inside

For y=f(g(x)), the chain rule says y′=f′(g(x))·g′(x). Differentiate the outer function while leaving the inner expression untouched; then multiply by the derivative of the inner expression.

Spotting the layers

In (3x+1)⁵, the outside operation is “fifth power” and the inside is 3x+1. In sin(x²), the outside is sine and the inside is x².

Units explain multiplication

If temperature changes 2 degrees per mile and distance changes 30 miles per hour, temperature changes (2 degrees/mile)(30 miles/hour)=60 degrees/hour. The middle unit cancels.

Worked Example

Problem: Differentiate y=(3x²+1)⁴.

1 Name the inside u=3x²+1. Then y=u⁴.

2 Differentiate the outside: dy/du=4u³.

3 Differentiate the inside: du/dx=6x.

4 Multiply and replace u.

Answer: y′=24x(3x²+1)³.

Common Mistakes

Differentiating the outside but forgetting the inner derivative.

Changing the inner expression while differentiating the outer layer.

Expanding a large power when the chain rule is shorter.

Practice: Do It Yourself

1. Differentiate (2x+5)⁷.

2. Differentiate sin(x³).

3. Differentiate e^(4x).

4. If A=πr² and r changes at 3 cm/s, write dA/dt in terms of r.

CHAPTER IN ONE BREATH For nested functions: derivative of the outside, evaluated at the inside, times derivative of the inside.

sections.title: CHAPTER 8
sections.html:
CHAPTER 8

Using Derivatives in Real Life

YOUR GOAL Use derivatives to optimize, describe motion, and approximate change.

The Big Idea

A derivative becomes powerful when you translate it back into the story. It can locate the cheapest design, the highest profit, the fastest change, or the moment motion reverses.

Finding peaks and valleys

Candidates occur where f′(x)=0 or f′ is undefined. Test each candidate and relevant endpoints. A sign change from + to − signals a local maximum; − to + signals a local minimum.

Motion

Position s(t) gives velocity v(t)=s′(t), and velocity gives acceleration a(t)=v′(t)=s″(t). Positive velocity means movement in the positive direction; positive acceleration means velocity is increasing—not necessarily that the object is moving forward.

Linear approximation

Near x=a, a smooth function behaves almost like its tangent line: f(x)≈f(a)+f′(a)(x−a). This turns a hard nearby calculation into an easy one.

Worked Example

Problem: A rectangle has perimeter 40. Find dimensions that maximize area.

1 Let length=x. Since 2x+2w=40, width=20−x.

2 Area A=x(20−x)=20x−x².

3 Differentiate: A′=20−2x.

4 Set A′=0: 20−2x=0, so x=10.

5 Then width=20−10=10. Endpoints give zero area, so this interior point is the maximum.

Answer: A 10-by-10 square, with maximum area 100 square units.

Common Mistakes

Finding a critical number but not checking whether it is max or min.

Ignoring physical restrictions such as positive length or limited time.

Confusing velocity with acceleration.

Practice: Do It Yourself

1. Find critical numbers of f(x)=x²−6x+5.

2. For s(t)=t³−6t²+9t, find v(t).

3. Use linear approximation at x=4 to estimate √4.1. Hint: f(x)=√x.

4. A 20-by-20 sheet loses squares of side x at each corner to make an open box. Write, but do not solve, the volume function.

CHAPTER IN ONE BREATH Differentiate the model, solve for important rates or critical points, then interpret and verify the result in context.

sections.title: CHAPTER 9
sections.html:
CHAPTER 9

Antiderivatives: Running Change Backward

YOUR GOAL Recover a quantity when you know its rate of change.

The Big Idea

Differentiation asks “what is the rate?” Antidifferentiation asks “what quantity has this rate?” Because constants disappear under differentiation, every indefinite integral needs +C.

Reverse the power rule

Since d/dx[xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)]=xⁿ, we have ∫xⁿ dx=xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)+C for n≠−1. Add one to the exponent, then divide by the new exponent.

Why +C matters

The derivatives of x², x²+5, and x²−100 are all 2x. A rate alone cannot reveal the starting level. An initial condition determines C.

A special case

The power rule cannot handle x⁻¹ because dividing by n+1 would mean dividing by zero. Instead, ∫(1/x)dx=ln|x|+C.

Worked Example

Problem: Find F(x) if F′(x)=6x²−4x+3 and F(0)=7.

1 Integrate term by term: ∫6x²dx=2x³, ∫−4x dx=−2x², and ∫3dx=3x.

2 Write F(x)=2x³−2x²+3x+C.

3 Use F(0)=7: 7=C.

Answer: F(x)=2x³−2x²+3x+7.

Common Mistakes

Forgetting +C.

Subtracting one from the exponent instead of adding one.

Using the power rule on 1/x.

Practice: Do It Yourself

1. Find ∫(4x³−6x+2)dx.

2. Find ∫cos x dx.

3. If v(t)=6t and s(0)=4, find s(t).

4. Differentiate your answer to problem 1 to check it.

CHAPTER IN ONE BREATH An antiderivative reverses differentiation; +C represents the unknown starting level.

sections.title: CHAPTER 10
sections.html:
CHAPTER 10

The Definite Integral: Adding Tiny Pieces

YOUR GOAL Understand an integral as accumulation and signed area.

The Big Idea

Suppose a rate changes every moment. You can still find the total by multiplying rate × tiny interval and adding all pieces. The definite integral is the limit of that increasingly accurate sum.

From rectangles to exact accumulation

Split [a,b] into narrow widths Δx. Each rectangle contributes approximately f(x)Δx. Adding gives a Riemann sum. As the widest rectangle shrinks toward zero, the sum approaches ∫ₐᵇf(x)dx.

Signed area

Area above the x-axis counts positive; area below counts negative. Therefore a definite integral is net signed area. Total geometric area requires splitting at crossings and making each piece positive.

Units

If f is gallons per minute and dx is minutes, f(x)dx has gallons. Integration multiplies the rate unit by the input unit, producing accumulated quantity.

Worked Example

Problem: Evaluate ∫₀² x dx geometrically.

1 The graph y=x from 0 to 2 forms a right triangle under the line.

2 Its base is 2 and height is 2.

3 Triangle area=(1/2)(base)(height).

Answer: 2 square units.

Common Mistakes

Treating signed area as always positive.

Forgetting the bounds on a definite integral.

Believing dx is decoration; it identifies the variable and carries the interval idea.

Practice: Do It Yourself

1. Use geometry to evaluate ∫₀⁴ 3 dx.

2. If f(x)=−2 on [1,5], evaluate the integral.

3. A pump runs at r(t) gallons/minute. Explain ∫₀¹⁰r(t)dt.

4. Approximate ∫₀²x²dx using two right-endpoint rectangles of width 1.

CHAPTER IN ONE BREATH A definite integral adds infinitely many tiny contributions and represents net accumulation.

sections.title: CHAPTER 11
sections.html:
CHAPTER 11

The Fundamental Theorem: The Great Bridge

YOUR GOAL Connect derivatives and integrals as inverse processes.

The Big Idea

The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus is the course’s central surprise: accumulation and instantaneous change undo each other. It converts a difficult infinite sum into endpoint subtraction.

sections.title: Part 1: accumulation has a derivative
sections.html:
Part 1: accumulation has a derivative

If A(x)=∫ₐˣf(t)dt, then A′(x)=f(x), provided f is continuous. Adding one more tiny slice changes accumulated area at a rate equal to the slice’s height.

Part 2: evaluate with antiderivatives

If F′=f, then ∫ₐᵇf(x)dx=F(b)−F(a). Find any antiderivative, plug in the upper endpoint, then subtract the lower endpoint.

The Net Change Theorem

If Q′(t) is the rate of change of Q, then Q(b)−Q(a)=∫ₐᵇQ′(t)dt. Total change equals accumulated rate.

Worked Example

Problem: Evaluate ∫₁³ 2x dx.

1 Find an antiderivative: F(x)=x².

2 Evaluate the upper endpoint: F(3)=9.

3 Evaluate the lower endpoint: F(1)=1.

4 Subtract lower from upper.

Answer: 8.

Common Mistakes

Writing F(a)−F(b) instead of upper minus lower.

Adding +C in a definite-integral calculation; the constants cancel.

Confusing ∫ₐˣf(t)dt with f(x). The first is an accumulation function.

Practice: Do It Yourself

1. Evaluate ∫₀² 3x² dx.

2. Evaluate ∫₀^π sin x dx.

3. If A(x)=∫₁ˣ(t²+1)dt, find A′(x).

4. A population changes at P′(t). Explain P(10)−P(2) as an integral.

CHAPTER IN ONE BREATH Differentiation measures local change; integration accumulates change; the Fundamental Theorem proves they undo each other.

sections.title: CHAPTER 12
sections.html:
CHAPTER 12

Integration Tools You Actually Need

YOUR GOAL Recognize substitution and integration by parts.

The Big Idea

Integration is pattern recognition. Unlike differentiation, there is no single rule that always works. Begin by simplifying, then look for a chain-rule pattern or a product pattern.

Substitution: reverse chain rule

When an integral contains an inner expression and its derivative, let u equal the inner expression. Replace du with its derivative times dx. Then integrate in u and substitute back.

Integration by parts: reverse product rule

From (uv)′=u′v+uv′ comes ∫u dv=uv−∫v du. It is useful for products such as x·eˣ or x·sin x. Choose u so differentiating it makes it simpler.

A decision ladder

First simplify algebraically. Next try the basic antiderivative table. Then look for inside-function × derivative (substitution). For a stubborn product, try parts. Always differentiate the result to check.

Worked Example

Problem: Evaluate ∫2x(x²+1)³ dx.

1 Choose u=x²+1 because it is the inner expression.

2 Then du=2x dx, which is exactly the remaining factor.

3 Rewrite as ∫u³du.

4 Integrate: u⁴/4+C.

5 Replace u.

Answer: (x²+1)⁴/4+C.

Common Mistakes

Choosing u but failing to replace the entire integral.

Forgetting to return from u to x in an indefinite integral.

Using a complicated method before simplifying.

Practice: Do It Yourself

1. Evaluate ∫3x²(x³+4)⁵dx.

2. Evaluate ∫x eˣ dx using parts.

3. Evaluate ∫(2x)/(x²+5) dx.

4. Differentiate your answer to problem 3.

CHAPTER IN ONE BREATH Integration tools reverse familiar derivative patterns; substitution reverses the chain rule and parts reverses the product rule.

sections.title: CHAPTER 13
sections.html:
CHAPTER 13

Motion, Growth, Area, and Averages

YOUR GOAL Translate real situations into derivative and integral models.

The Big Idea

Calculus is useful because it lets rates, totals, and shapes speak to one another. The essential skill is translation: name the quantity, identify its units, and decide whether the problem asks for a rate or an accumulation.

Motion and distance

Displacement is ∫v(t)dt and may cancel opposite directions. Total distance is ∫|v(t)|dt, so split where velocity changes sign. Acceleration is the derivative of velocity.

Average value

The average value of f on [a,b] is (1/(b−a))∫ₐᵇf(x)dx. It is accumulated output divided by interval length—the continuous version of ordinary average.

Growth models

Exponential growth satisfies P′=kP: the rate is proportional to the amount present. Its solution is P(t)=P₀eᵏᵗ. Positive k means growth; negative k means decay.

Worked Example

Problem: Velocity is v(t)=2t−4 m/s for 0≤t≤5. Find displacement.

1 Displacement is the integral of velocity: ∫₀⁵(2t−4)dt.

2 An antiderivative is t²−4t.

3 Evaluate: [25−20]−[0−0].

Answer: 5 meters. Note: total distance is larger because velocity is negative before t=2 and positive after.

Common Mistakes

Using displacement when the question asks for total distance.

Mixing units across a model.

Using a derivative when the question asks for a total accumulated amount.

Practice: Do It Yourself

1. For v(t)=3t², find displacement from t=0 to 2.

2. Find the average value of f(x)=x on [0,4].

3. A bacteria culture follows P(t)=100e^(0.2t). Find P′(t).

4. For v(t)=t−1 on [0,3], set up the integral for total distance.

CHAPTER IN ONE BREATH Translate the story with units: derivatives answer “how fast now?” and integrals answer “how much in total?”

sections.title: CHAPTER 14
sections.html:
CHAPTER 14

The Whole Course on One Map

YOUR GOAL Choose the correct calculus idea and solve with confidence.

The Big Idea

Calculus is not a bag of unrelated tricks. It is a two-part language: derivatives describe local change, and integrals describe total accumulation. Limits make both exact; the Fundamental Theorem connects them.

The four-question method

1. What quantity is given? 2. What quantity is requested? 3. Is this about approaching, instant rate, or total accumulation? 4. What units should the answer have? These questions often reveal the operation before any algebra begins.

A reliable solution structure

Name variables and units. Write the governing formula. Substitute carefully. Simplify one line at a time. Check sign, size, and units. Finally, state the answer in a sentence.

What mastery looks like

Mastery does not mean memorizing every integral. It means recognizing structure, selecting a tool, checking the result, and explaining what it means. If you can teach the idea simply, you understand it.

Worked Example

Problem: Water enters a tank at r(t)=4+t gallons/minute. How much enters from minute 0 to minute 6, and what is the inflow rate at minute 6?

1 “How much” asks for accumulation: ∫₀⁶(4+t)dt.

2 Antiderivative: 4t+t²/2. Evaluate: 24+18=42 gallons.

3 “Rate at minute 6” asks for the function value r(6)=10.

Answer: 42 gallons enter; at minute 6 the rate is 10 gallons per minute.

Common Mistakes

Starting computation before identifying what is asked.

Reporting a number without units or interpretation.

Assuming every problem needs a complicated technique.

Practice: Do It Yourself

1. Classify each as limit, derivative, or integral: instant speed; total fuel used; nearby behavior.

2. A cost function is C(q)=q²+20q+500. Find marginal cost C′(q).

3. Evaluate ∫₀³(2x+1)dx.

4. Explain the Fundamental Theorem in one sentence without symbols.

CHAPTER IN ONE BREATH Limits make “infinitely close” precise; derivatives measure instant change; integrals accumulate; the Fundamental Theorem shows the last two are inverse processes.

sections.html:
APPENDIX A

Answer Key

Chapter 1

1. 2x+10

2. (x−4)(x+4)

sections.title: APPENDIX B
sections.html:
APPENDIX B

Formula Sheet

Idea

Formula

Average rate

[f(b)−f(a)]/(b−a)

Derivative definition

f′(x)=lim h→0 [f(x+h)−f(x)]/h

Power rule

d/dx(xⁿ)=nxⁿ⁻¹

Product rule

(uv)′=u′v+uv′

Quotient rule

(u/v)′=(u′v−uv′)/v²

Chain rule

d/dx f(g(x))=f′(g(x))g′(x)

Basic integral

∫xⁿdx=xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)+C, n≠−1

Fundamental Theorem

∫ₐᵇf(x)dx=F(b)−F(a), where F′=f

Average value

f_avg=(1/(b−a))∫ₐᵇf(x)dx

Linear approximation

f(x)≈f(a)+f′(a)(x−a)

A 30-Day Learning Plan

Days 1–3: Chapter 1; repair algebra gaps.

Days 4–5: Chapters 2–3; functions and graphs.

Days 6–8: Chapter 4; limits.

Days 9–12: Chapters 5–6; derivative meaning and rules.

Days 13–15: Chapters 7–8; chain rule and applications.

Days 16–18: Chapters 9–10; antiderivatives and accumulation.

Days 19–21: Chapters 11–12; Fundamental Theorem and tools.

Days 22–24: Chapter 13; applications.

Days 25–27: Redo every missed practice problem.

Days 28–29: Teach each chapter aloud in two minutes.

Day 30: Complete Chapter 14 and write your one-page calculus map.

Final Self-Test

☐ Can I explain a limit without saying “plug it in”?

☐ Can I distinguish function value from derivative value?

☐ Can I explain a derivative as both tangent slope and instant rate?

☐ Can I explain an integral as both signed area and accumulated quantity?

☐ Can I state the Fundamental Theorem in my own words?

☐ Do I check units and meaning after calculating?

THE FINISH LINE You understand calculus when the symbols point to a picture, a rate, or a total—and you can explain which one and why.
